summary: AlterEcho is a smart geospatial platform that takes elevation data from NASA and planetary missions to measure how closely Earth’s landscapes actually match landing sites on Mars and the Moon. Instead of picking analog test sites based on general descriptions and guesswork, our system uses a reproducible mathematical framework (analogue-method-v1.0) to compare the slope and height distributions of a 10 km landscape against planetary targets on a unified 60-meter grid. It calculates precise similarity scores, checks how ordinary background Earth windows compare, and builds in strict error floors to flag when data differences are too small to tell apart. We built a complete end-to-end tool: processing multi-source elevation rasters, filtering out human structures, running dozens of sensitivity checks, and reliably separating gentle analog plains from rugged mountain terrain. This matters because choosing where to test space missions requires rigorous, transparent data. By combining real space agency data with statistical distribution comparisons and uncertainty controls, AlterEcho cuts through subjective bias and gives researchers a reliable first-pass screen for planetary analog sites.
details:
AlterEcho — Project Details

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

1. Project Overview

AlterEcho is a planetary terrain comparison platform designed to identify places on Earth that have similar physical terrain characteristics to selected locations on Mars and the Moon.

The platform uses real elevation data from NASA and USGS sources to compare landscapes at the same scale. Instead of relying only on visual similarities or general descriptions, it measures terrain properties mathematically and provides a score showing how closely two locations resemble each other.

Its main purpose is to help researchers, planetary scientists and mission planners explore potential Earth analog sites that could be useful for studying planetary environments and preparing for future exploration missions.

The platform currently focuses on terrain resemblance, but its framework can be expanded to include additional environmental and geological features.

2. The Problem It Addresses

Before sending rovers, instruments and scientific equipment to another planet, researchers need to test them in environments on Earth.

These locations are known as planetary analog sites. They help researchers understand how equipment and scientific procedures may perform under conditions similar to those found on Mars or other planetary bodies.

However, selecting an analog site is challenging. Two locations may look similar in photographs but have very different terrain characteristics. Likewise, a location that resembles Mars in terms of elevation may not have similar geological or environmental conditions.

AlterEcho addresses this problem by providing a measurable way to compare terrain. It helps users understand:

  • How closely an Earth location resembles a selected planetary location.
  • Which terrain characteristics are responsible for the similarity.
  • Whether the result is unusual compared with ordinary Earth landscapes.
  • Whether the available elevation data is reliable enough to distinguish between two locations.
  • Which areas deserve further scientific investigation.

3. Main Features and Capabilities

A. Earth-to-Planet Terrain Comparison

AlterEcho compares selected Earth locations with reference areas on Mars and the Moon.

The current research includes seven Earth study areas:

  • Craters of the Moon, USA
  • Hanksville, Utah, USA
  • Dallol, Ethiopia
  • Atacama Desert, Chile
  • Meteor Crater, USA
  • Upper Mustang, Nepal
  • Ladakh, India

It also includes five Mars reference areas:

  • Jezero Crater
  • Gale Crater
  • Elysium Planitia
  • Gusev Crater
  • Eberswalde Crater

A lunar south-pole reference is also included for distance comparisons.

Each comparison uses a 10 km study window and a common 60 m analysis grid. This helps ensure that the comparison is made at a consistent scale.

B. Terrain Analysis

The platform studies measurable characteristics of the land using elevation models.

Its current analysis includes:

  • Slope: Measures the steepness of the land. Why it matters: Helps identify flat and steep terrain.
  • Relative elevation: Measures elevation compared with the area's median elevation. Why it matters: Measures how terrain rises and falls.
  • Local relief: Measures the difference between the highest and lowest nearby elevations. Why it matters: Shows larger variations in the landscape.
  • Roughness: Measures variation in elevation across a small neighbourhood. Why it matters: Helps describe surface unevenness.

Slope and relative elevation are currently used in the main scoring formula. Local relief and roughness are retained as additional diagnostic measurements.

This allows the platform to compare more than just the average height of two locations.

C. Mathematical Similarity Scoring

One of AlterEcho's main features is its ability to convert terrain differences into a numerical similarity index.

It uses the Wasserstein distance to compare the complete distributions of terrain measurements instead of comparing only their averages.

The distance is then converted into a similarity value:

Dₖ = dₖ / τₖ

sₖ = 2^(−Dₖ²)

Where:

  • dₖ = measured difference between the two terrain distributions.
  • τₖ = reference tolerance calculated from ordinary Earth landscapes.
  • Dₖ = normalized difference.
  • sₖ = similarity value between 0 and 1.

The final terrain index combines slope and relative elevation with equal weights:

Aobs = 100 × (0.5 · sslope + 0.5 · srel)

The result is an experimental index from 0 to 100. A higher score indicates greater similarity in the measured terrain characteristics.

Important: The score is not a probability, percentage of planetary equivalence, or certification that two locations are scientifically identical.

D. Background Comparison

A high similarity score does not automatically mean that a location is unique.

AlterEcho addresses this by comparing each result against 88 ordinary Earth terrain windows.

It calculates the percentage of background locations that achieve an equal or higher score.

For example, if a location has a background share of 17%, it means that 17% of the 88 background windows scored at least as high.

This gives users a better understanding of whether a match is unusual or whether many ordinary landscapes produce similar results.

E. Reliability and Uncertainty Checks

The platform includes checks designed to prevent misleading comparisons.

These include:

  • Moving study windows by 2 km to test how much their placement affects the results.
  • Comparing alternative elevation datasets to identify differences caused by data sources.
  • Testing different analysis resolutions.
  • Changing feature weights and tolerances under alternative scenarios.
  • Reporting when two locations cannot be reliably distinguished.

When scenario ranges overlap, locations are treated as tied rather than forcing an unreliable ranking.

The platform also reports evidence coverage, which indicates how much of the planned comparison has actually been measured.

F. Interactive Exploration and Reports

The project includes a working application concept that allows users to select a planetary reference and explore matching Earth locations.

Its demonstrated workflow includes:

  1. Selecting a Mars reference location.
  2. Comparing available Earth study areas.
  3. Viewing ranked terrain matches and ties.
  4. Checking the background share and scenario range.
  5. Exploring the supporting evidence.
  6. Accessing detailed reports and JSON results.

The platform is also designed to allow users to explore other areas of Earth rather than being restricted to the existing study locations.

4. What Can AlterEcho Be Used For?

Planetary mission preparation

Researchers could use the platform as an initial screening tool when searching for Earth locations where rover equipment, instruments and field procedures can be tested.

Finding potential analog environments

Scientists could identify areas with terrain characteristics similar to selected Martian locations and investigate whether they are useful for specific experiments.

Scientific research

Researchers could use the measurements and comparison results as an additional source of evidence when studying planetary landscapes.

Rover and instrument testing

The platform could help identify locations with particular terrain characteristics for testing mobility systems, navigation methods and scientific instruments. A terrain match alone, however, cannot establish operational safety.

Education and research exploration

Students and educators could use the platform to explore how the surfaces of Earth and other planetary bodies differ, and how elevation data can be used in planetary science.

5. Future Development and Potential

AlterEcho has the potential to develop into a more comprehensive planetary environment comparison platform. Its current terrain-based approach provides a starting point for adding more scientific measurements.

The following are proposed future developments, not capabilities that have already been validated.

A. Advanced Landform Recognition

The current system compares terrain distributions, but it does not fully describe the arrangement of individual landforms.

Future versions could identify and compare:

  • River channels and ancient drainage systems.
  • Impact craters and their rims.
  • Ridges and valleys.
  • Deltas and sedimentary formations.
  • Volcanic structures.
  • Erosion patterns.

This could help distinguish between locations that have similar elevation distributions but very different physical landscapes.

B. Geological and Environmental Analysis

Future versions could incorporate additional datasets to compare:

  • Surface mineral composition.
  • Rock and soil characteristics.
  • Temperature variations.
  • Water and ice distribution.
  • Geological formations.
  • Surface weathering and erosion.

Combining these measurements with terrain analysis could provide a more complete picture of how useful a location might be for a particular scientific investigation.

These features would require appropriate data, comparable measurements and independent validation.

C. More Planetary Reference Locations

The current project focuses mainly on Mars, with an additional lunar reference.

Future development could include more planetary study areas, such as:

  • Oxia Planum, Mars.
  • Meridiani Planum, Mars.
  • Additional Martian crater and volcanic regions.
  • More lunar landing and exploration regions.

This would expand the number of possible comparisons and make the platform useful for a wider range of research questions.

D. AI-Based Landform Classification

Machine learning could eventually be used to recognise landforms from satellite images and elevation data.

A future version could help identify terrain patterns automatically, classify landscape types and suggest locations for further comparison.

This would require a properly labelled training dataset and testing against independent expert assessments.

E. Mission-Specific Recommendations

Rather than producing one general terrain score, future versions could provide comparisons based on the purpose of a mission.

For example:This could make the platform more useful because a location suitable for geological research may not necessarily be suitable for rover mobility or landing operations.

F. Global Terrain Exploration

A long-term goal could be to allow users to select almost any location on Earth and compare it with a selected planetary reference.

This could turn AlterEcho into a global exploration tool where researchers can investigate potential analog environments without being limited to a predefined list of locations.

6. Current Results and Demonstrated Performance

The current research demonstrates that the platform can process real elevation datasets, compare terrain distributions and produce reproducible numerical results.

Some of the key findings include:

  • Craters of the Moon vs. Jezero Crater — Terrain index: 98.2
  • Atacama Desert (south) vs. Jezero Crater — Terrain index: 97.9
  • Hanksville vs. Jezero Crater — Terrain index: 97.4
  • Meteor Crater vs. Jezero Crater — Terrain index: 95.1
  • Dallol vs. Jezero Crater — Terrain index: 88.6
  • Upper Mustang vs. Jezero Crater — Terrain index: 0.6
  • Ladakh vs. Jezero Crater — Terrain index: 0.0


These values demonstrate how the system distinguishes between broad terrain classes. They do not establish that the highest-scoring locations are the best overall planetary analogs.

One important finding is that approximately 42–49% of ordinary background Earth windows also score 90 or higher against the Mars references. This shows why the platform needs background comparisons and why a high score should not be interpreted on its own.

Upper Mustang and Ladakh have much steeper terrain distributions than the selected Mars references, which explains their low scores. This does not mean they lack scientific value; they may be useful for research questions involving rugged terrain.

7. Data Sources and Technical Foundation

AlterEcho uses real elevation datasets rather than manually created terrain measurements.

  • Craters of the Moon vs. Jezero Crater — Terrain index: 98.2
  • Atacama Desert (south) vs. Jezero Crater — Terrain index: 97.9
  • Hanksville vs. Jezero Crater — Terrain index: 97.4
  • Meteor Crater vs. Jezero Crater — Terrain index: 95.1
  • Dallol vs. Jezero Crater — Terrain index: 88.6
  • Upper Mustang vs. Jezero Crater — Terrain index: 0.6
  • Ladakh vs. Jezero Crater — Terrain index: 0.0

The research uses Python for data processing and numerical analysis, with NumPy and Rasterio for calculations and raster handling. FastAPI is included in the technical software stack.

The project also maintains source information, processing versions and SHA-256 checksums to support reproducibility.

8. Limitations and Scientific Considerations

AlterEcho is currently an experimental terrain comparison platform. Its results should be used as an initial screening tool rather than a final scientific judgement.

The current system:

  • Measures terrain, not complete geological or environmental similarity.
  • Does not establish habitability or the presence of life.
  • Cannot certify landing safety or rover suitability.
  • Does not measure mineral composition, water availability or soil strength.
  • Has not yet undergone independent expert-labelled validation.
  • Cannot reliably rank locations when their scenario ranges overlap.

The lunar reference also fails the project's resolution-floor requirement, so it provides terrain distances rather than a final similarity index.

These limitations are important because they define what the current platform can reliably do and what future development needs to address.

9. Overall Vision

AlterEcho aims to make planetary terrain comparison more measurable, transparent and accessible.

Its current capabilities provide a way to compare real landscapes using elevation data, mathematical analysis and uncertainty checks. Its future potential lies in combining terrain analysis with landform recognition, geological information, environmental datasets and AI-based classification.

The long-term vision is to create a platform where researchers can select a planetary location, define their research objective and explore suitable Earth environments using multiple forms of scientific evidence.

Rather than simply identifying places that look like Mars, AlterEcho aims to help explain how similar they are, what makes them similar, how reliable the comparison is, and what further research is needed.
